## So far{.smaller}

| Method | Population Parameter | Sample Statistic | Theoretical Distribution | Degrees of Freedom |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Difference in proportions | x | x | x | x |
| Difference in means | x | x | x | x |
| Chi-square test of independence | x | x | x | x |

## So far{.smaller} 

| Method | Population Parameter | Sample Statistic | Theoretical Distribution | Degrees of Freedom |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Difference in proportions | $p_1-p_2$ | $\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2$ | $Z \approx N(0,1)$ | N/A |
| Difference in means | $\mu_1-\mu_2$ | $\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2$ | $T \sim t_{df}$ | $df$ estimated conservative $min(n_1-1,n_2-1)$ |
| Chi-square test of independence | Association between two categorical variables | $\chi^2=\sum \frac{(O-E)^2}{E}$ | $\chi^2 \sim \chi^2_{df}$ | $(r-1)(c-1)$ |

What are the variables?

## Extension 

ANOVA is an extension from difference in means, where the test statistic is the variability within group vs the variability across groups. 

What do I mean by variability?

## Example 

```{r}
#| echo: false
# 1. Load necessary libraries
library(tidyverse)

# --- Data Generation ---

# Set parameters for the simulation
set.seed(42) # For reproducibility
N <- 50      # Sample size per group
std_dev <- 2 # Low variability within groups

# Generate data for three groups (High variability across means)
data_a <- rnorm(N, mean = 10, sd = std_dev)
data_b <- rnorm(N, mean = 25, sd = std_dev)
data_c <- rnorm(N, mean = 40, sd = std_dev)

# 2. Structure data in long format (tidy data)
df_variability <- tibble(
  Group = factor(c(rep("A (Mean=10)", N),
                   rep("B (Mean=25)", N),
                   rep("C (Mean=40)", N))),
  Value = c(data_a, data_b, data_c)
)

# 3. Create the side-by-side boxplots using ggplot2
ggplot(df_variability, aes(x = Group, y = Value, fill = Group)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.5) + # Add the boxplots
  labs(
    title = "Boxplots Demonstrating High Between-Group and Low Within-Group Variability",
    x = "Group",
    y = "Value (Units)"
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d() + # Use a pleasant color palette
  theme_minimal() + # Use a clean theme
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5), # Center the title
    legend.position = "none" # Hide the legend as Group is on the x-axis
  )
```

## Normality

Previously, with a quantitative response, we checked the normality assumption by looking at our sample size. If our sample size was $\ge$ 30, the CLT kicks in and we can trust that the sampling distribution of the difference in means is roughly normally distributed. However, as we will see, our statistic is a ratio of mean squares, not simply a standardized difference between two means.

**Takeaway**: With non-normal data, large samples can make ANOVA more robust, but the CLT alone does not guarantee an exact F-distribution.

## Plants q-q

```{r}
#| echo: false
# 1. Load necessary libraries
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(qqplotr) # A specialized package for ggplot2 Q-Q plots

# The PlantGrowth dataset is built-in, so no need to load data manually.

# 2. Convert 'group' to a factor (it already is, but good practice)
PlantGrowth$group <- factor(PlantGrowth$group)

library(tidyverse)

qq_data <- PlantGrowth %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  arrange(weight, .by_group = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(
    rank = row_number(),
    theoretical = qnorm((rank - 0.5) / n())
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

# Calculate a separate reference line for each group
line_data <- qq_data %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  summarise(
    intercept = mean(weight) - sd(weight) * 0,
    slope = sd(weight),
    x_min = min(theoretical),
    x_max = max(theoretical),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    y_min = intercept + slope * x_min,
    y_max = intercept + slope * x_max
  )

ggplot(qq_data, aes(x = theoretical, y = weight, color = group)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_segment(
    data = line_data,
    aes(
      x = x_min, y = y_min,
      xend = x_max, yend = y_max,
      color = group
    ),
    linetype = "dashed",
    inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ group, ncol = 3) +
  labs(
    title = "Normal Q-Q Plot for PlantGrowth Data by Group",
    x = "Theoretical Quantiles",
    y = "Sample Quantiles"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

```


-- What are Sample Quantiles?

-- What are Theoretical Quantiles?

-- What are we looking for?

## Sample Quantiles 

These are values that we actually observe from our data set! 

These go on the y-axis of or normal q-q plot

## Theoretical Quantiles 

The theoretical quantiles are the quantiles we would expect to see if the data followed a normal distribution.

-- They represent the values predicted by a theoretical normal distribution.

-- They are plotted on the x-axis.

## Theoretical Quantiles{.smaller} 

-- Order our observed data from smallest to largest (rank)

-- Divide up the theoretical normal distribution into EQUAL corresponding quantiles, based on the ranks of our observations

-- Calculate the quantile value

$q_i = \Phi^{-1}\left(\dfrac{i-0.5}{n}\right)$

1. $q_i$ = theoretical quantile for observation $i$

2. $\Phi^{-1}$ = inverse standard normal CDF (the quantile function)

3. $i$ = rank of the observation, from smallest to largest

4. $n$ = sample size

## 

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

# Sample data, n = 10
x <- c(12, 15, 11, 18, 14, 13, 20, 16, 10, 17)

n <- length(x)

# Order the observed data and calculate theoretical quantiles
qq_data <- tibble(
  i = 1:n,
  sample_quantile = sort(x),
  probability = (i - 0.5) / n,
  theoretical_quantile = qnorm(probability)
)

# Plot theoretical normal distribution
ggplot() +
  stat_function(
    fun = dnorm,
    xlim = c(-3, 3),
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    data = qq_data,
    aes(xintercept = theoretical_quantile),
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "gray50"
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = qq_data,
    aes(x = theoretical_quantile, y = dnorm(theoretical_quantile)),
    size = 3
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Theoretical Quantiles for a Normal Q-Q Plot",
    subtitle = "n = 10: Each rank is paired with a theoretical normal quantile",
    x = "Theoretical normal quantile",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()


```

## Theoretical Quantiles 

```{r}
# 3. Create the Q-Q Plots for Each Group
# We use facet_wrap to separate the plots by the 'group' variable.
qq_plot_data <- ggplot(data = PlantGrowth, mapping = aes(sample = weight, color = group)) +
  # Use stat_qq_point to plot the observed quantiles
  stat_qq_point(size = 2) +
  # Use stat_qq_line to add the theoretical normal line
  stat_qq_line(line.color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  # Separate the plots by the 'group' factor
  facet_wrap(~ group, scales = "fixed", ncol = 3) +
  labs(
    title = "Normal Q-Q Plot for PlantGrowth Data by Group",
    x = "Theoretical Quantiles",
    y = "Sample Quantiles"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

# Print the plots
print(qq_plot_data)
```

So, how do we feel about our assumption?

## Guess the distribution 

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

set.seed(123)

left_skew_data <- tibble(
  x = -rlnorm(100, meanlog = 0, sdlog = 0.6)
)

# Calculate theoretical quantiles and ordered observations
qq_data <- left_skew_data %>%
  arrange(x) %>%
  mutate(
    theoretical = qnorm((row_number() - 0.5) / n())
  )

# Calculate a Q-Q reference line using the first and third quartiles
q_theory <- qnorm(c(0.25, 0.75))
q_sample <- quantile(qq_data$x, c(0.25, 0.75))

slope <- diff(q_sample) / diff(q_theory)
intercept <- q_sample[1] - slope * q_theory[1]

ggplot(qq_data, aes(x = theoretical, y = x)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_abline(
    intercept = intercept,
    slope = slope,
    color = "red",
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Normal Q-Q Plot: _______ Data",
    x = "Theoretical Normal Quantiles",
    y = "Sample Quantiles"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

## General Rule 

Points above the line: Observed values are larger than the line predicts at those theoretical quantiles.

Points below the line: Observed values are smaller than the line predicts at those theoretical quantiles.

## Summary 

Your qq-plots can take on many different shapes. There is not right/wrong cut-off. It's up to you to make a justifiable call

--    Right-skewed: The upper tail extends farther above the reference line than expected under normality.

--    Left-skewed: The lower tail extends farther below the reference line than expected under normality.

# Questions 


## Equal variance (New!)

The equal variance assumption (also called homogeneity of variance) in ANOVA means that the populations for all groups have the same variance, even if their means differ

$\sigma_1^2=\sigma_2^2=\cdots=\sigma_k^2$

$\sigma^2 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}(x_i-\mu)^2}{N}$

## Equal Variance 

```{r}
ggplot(PlantGrowth, aes(x = group, y = weight)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    x = "Treatment Group",
    y = "Plant Weight",
    title = "Compare Variability Across Groups"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

## Equal Variance 

```{r}
model <- aov(weight ~ group, data = PlantGrowth)

plot(
  fitted(model),
  residuals(model),
  xlab = "Fitted Values",
  ylab = "Residuals",
  main = "Residuals vs. Fitted Values"
)
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
```

What's a residual? 

What's a fitted value?

## Residual 

$e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i$

observed - fitted value 

in ANOVA, the fitted value (best guess) is just the mean! 

So, the residual in ANOVA is distance between individual values and their group mean

## Equal Variance 

```{r}
model <- aov(weight ~ group, data = PlantGrowth)

plot(
  fitted(model),
  residuals(model),
  xlab = "Fitted Values",
  ylab = "Residuals",
  main = "Residuals vs. Fitted Values"
)
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
```

How do we check the assumption?

## Equal Variance



```{r}
#| echo: false

PlantGrowth |>
  group_by(group) |>
  summarize(sd = sd(weight))

```

General rule: Is the largest sample standard deviation more than twice
the smallest sample standard deviation?

## Assumptions 

Independence ✓

Normality ✓

Equal Variance ✓ 

## New statistic

$F = \frac{\text{MS}_{\text{Between}}}{\text{MS}_{\text{Within}}}$

$\mathbf{F} = \frac{\frac{\text{SS}_{\text{Between}}}{k - 1}}{\frac{\text{SS}_{\text{Within}}}{N - k}}$

$\text{SS}_{\text{Between}} = \sum_{i=1}^{k} n_i (\bar{X}_i - \bar{X}_{\text{grand}})^2$

$\text{SS}_{\text{Within}} = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \sum_{j=1}^{n_i} (X_{ij} - \bar{X}_i)^2$

## Draw it out

What would this look like?

That is, draw out how each SS would be calculated.

## Plants

```{r}
#| echo: false
set.seed(123)
a <- PlantGrowth |>
  group_by(group) |>

PlantGrowth |>
  ggplot(
    aes(x = group, y = weight)) +
  geom_jitter(width = .1) + 
  facet_wrap(~ group) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 5.073, color = "red" , lwd = 1) +     
  geom_hline(data = a, aes(yintercept = mean), color = "blue", linetype = "solid") + 
  labs(title = "Anova example", 
       subtitle = "Red line is overall mean; blue lines are group means")

```

## F-distribution

[applet](https://www.stapplet.com/fdist.html)

A continuous, positively skewed probability distribution, characterized
by two degrees of freedom (numerator and denominator) that determine its
shape.

## Anova

Where did all of this come from?

The goal is not for you to be able to calculate these values by hand
(besides Df). The goal is for you to understand the relationships
between the values of the Anova table.

```{r}
#| echo: false

anova_model <- aov(weight ~ group, data = PlantGrowth)

summary(anova_model)
```

## Definitions {.smaller}

Degrees of Freedom (df) is the number of independent pieces of
information used to calculate the statistic

The Sum of Squares (SS) is a measure of total variability (between or
within)

The Mean Squares (MS) is an estimate ($s^2$) of the population variance
($\sigma^2$)

It's a generalized form of $s^2 = \frac{\sum(x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n-1}$

## Anova table

Where did we get df = 2 for between? Where did we get df = 27 for
within?

```{r}
#| echo: false

PlantGrowth |>
  group_by(group) |>
  summarise(n = n())
```

## degrees of freedom 

When we estimate the population (grand) mean, there are k-1 independent pieces of information 

When we estimate the population means within each group, there are n - k independent pieces of information


## Anova: MS {.smaller}

The Mean Squares (MS) is an estimate ($s^2$) of the population variance
($\sigma^2$)

It's a generalized form of $s^2 = \frac{\sum(x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n-1}$

In Anova, it's calculated by taking $\frac{SS}{df}$

```{r}
#| echo: false

anova_model <- aov(weight ~ group, data = PlantGrowth)

summary(anova_model)
```

## Anova: F-statistic

The whole goal of Anova is to compare the variability between groups vs
the variability within groups. How can we calculate our F-statistic?

```{r}
#| echo: false

anova_model <- aov(weight ~ group, data = PlantGrowth)

summary(anova_model)
```
